# Cryptanalysis by Measurement

Identifying and attacking a cipher by **measuring statistical properties of its output** rather than
by reasoning about its construction. You do not need the algorithm's specification to learn a great
deal from a ciphertext — you need a distribution to compare against.

This is the organising idea of labs 02–05 in [[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]], and the one
skill in that repository backed by numbers rather than by prose.

## The five measurements

| Measurement | What it exposes |
|---|---|
| **Entropy** (bits/symbol) | how close the output is to uniform — a strong cipher's output is near-maximal regardless of its input |
| **Character frequency histogram** | whether the output preserves the source language's letter distribution |
| **Autocorrelation** (coincidence index) | text against a shifted copy of itself; peaks at multiples of the key length |
| **Periodicity** | repeated fixed patterns, with an offset and a period |
| **N-grams** (bi/tri/…) | block-level structure that single-character frequency misses |

Autocorrelation is the sharpest of the five because it recovers a *parameter* — the key length — not
just a classification. Once the period of a polyalphabetic cipher is known, the problem collapses into
that many independent monoalphabetic substitutions, each of which frequency analysis solves.

## What the measurements actually showed

The lab-02 entropy figures over one fixed English plaintext are the clearest single result in the
repository, because they rank the classical ciphers without any attack being run:

| Cipher | Ciphertext entropy (bits/symbol) |
|---|---|
| ADFGVX | 2.26 |
| Caesar | 4.15 |
| Playfair | 4.47 |
| Vigenère (short key) | 4.54 |
| Vigenère (longer key) | 4.62 |
| Hill (2×2 / 5×5) | 4.63 / 4.68 |
| Homophonic substitution | 7.77 (of a maximum 8.00) |

Substitution ciphers barely move entropy at all — they permute symbols without flattening the
distribution, which is precisely why frequency analysis defeats them. Homophonic substitution, which
maps one plaintext letter onto many ciphertext symbols, nearly reaches maximum entropy and defeats the
same tool. **Entropy is measuring the defence, not the secrecy.**

Lab 03 repeats the experiment against modern block ciphers with three plaintexts of deliberately
different diversity — homogeneous, medium, highly diversified. Under AES and DES in CBC, plaintext
entropies of 0.00, 4.04 and 3.97 all produce ciphertext entropy around 7.80–7.83. **A modern cipher's
output entropy is independent of its input's.** That single observation is the boundary between the
two halves of the course: the measurements that break classical ciphers stop working exactly here.

## The limits, recorded honestly

The lab-05 exercises apply the same instinct to modern algorithms — brute force against AES at
128/192/256 bits, varying how many key bits are unknown and where — and the report states plainly that
no exact key was recovered, only a direction. That is the correct outcome and the report does not
dress it up. Compare the theory answers in the same labs, several of which are generic filler; the
measured work is the part this page cites.

The classical attack models the labs enumerate — ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext,
differential, linear, replay, and [[man-in-the-middle-attack]] — are the framework these measurements
sit inside. Two get their own treatment elsewhere:
[[symmetric-vs-asymmetric-cryptography]] for why bulk data is not encrypted with a public-key
primitive, and [[rsa-and-integer-factorization]] for the number-theoretic attacks that replace
statistics entirely once the cipher is asymmetric.

## Scope note

Every technique here is described as a class of measurement. No ciphertext, key material, or
identifier-derived factorisation input from the labs appears in this wiki — see
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]] for the redaction rule.
